migrationNotes: Spine: a stuck bolt and a spanner. Distance and force both matter, a slanted push counts only for the part across the handle, a line through the pivot turns nothing, and moments about a pivot balance a see-saw.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): none. All ten questions are used.

lesson.title: Turning effect: moments

lead.text: Put a spanner on a stuck bolt and push on the end of the handle, at right angles to it. The bolt turns more easily when you push harder, and it turns more easily when the handle is longer. Engineers call the turning effect of a force about a point a moment. The point it turns about is the pivot, which here is the centre of the bolt.

A moment is found by multiplying the force by the distance from the pivot, measured at right angles to the push: M = F × d. With the force in newtons and the distance in metres, the moment comes out in newton-metres (N·m). A 100 N push 0.2 m from the bolt gives 20 N·m, and the same push 0.4 m from the bolt gives 40 N·m. Doubling the distance doubles the moment. Both cases are in the picture below.

afterFigure.text: Moments can turn either way, so they carry a sign. Here anticlockwise is positive and clockwise is negative. For a single push the sign hardly matters, but it will once several forces act on the same body. In practice, distance helps as much as force does. To loosen a tight nut with the least effort, push as far from it as you can, at right angles to the handle.

lead.text: Moment is force times distance, so each option below changes one of them.
The push is at right angles to the handle, so the full distance to the bolt counts.

So far the push has been at right angles to the handle. Real pushes are rarely so tidy, and a hand may push the spanner at a slant. As the first lesson showed, the force then has two components: one across the handle and one along it. The part along the handle only shoves the spanner towards the bolt or away from it, and does nothing to turn the bolt. Only the part across the handle turns it.

For a force F at an angle θ to the handle, the turning part is F sin θ. The moment is then M = F sin θ × d, where d is still the full distance from the bolt along the handle. A quick check is the right-angled case. At θ = 90° the sine is 1, and the formula gives F × d again. As the push swings round towards the handle, the moment shrinks.

afterFigure.text: The picture compares a push at right angles with a slanted push of the same size at the same place. The slanted one turns the bolt less, because less of it acts across the handle.

steps.headline: A 90 N push acts at 30° to a spanner, 0.4 m from the bolt. Find the moment about the bolt.

lead.text: Here is the slanted push in full, with the reason for each line.

workedSteps.text: Only the part of the push across the spanner turns it.
Multiply by the full distance along the spanner.

steps.headline: The 150 N push is now at 30° to the spanner, still 0.3 m from the bolt. Find the moment.

lead.text: Compare the answer with the 45 N·m you found for the same push at right angles.

workedSteps.text: Take the part of the push across the spanner.
Multiply that part by the 0.3 m distance, in N·m.

steps.headline: The line the force acts along

lead.text: There is a second way to see the same rule. Draw the line that the force acts along, called its line of action, and measure from the pivot straight across to that line. The shortest distance, at right angles to the line, is the perpendicular distance. That is the d in M = F × d. For a push at right angles to the handle it equals the distance along the handle. For a slanted push it is shorter, which is why the slanted push turns less.

One consequence is worth stating plainly. If the line of action passes through the pivot, the perpendicular distance is zero, and so is the moment, whatever the size of the force. Try to open a door by pushing on its hinge and it will not budge. Engineers use this the other way round. An unknown force is given a line through the point they take moments about, and it drops out of the equation.

diagram.alt: A spanner on a bolt with a long dashed line drawn along the push. In the first view the push is slanted and a short right-angled segment from the bolt to the dashed line marks the perpendicular distance. In the second the dashed line passes through the bolt, so the distance is zero.
diagram.caption: The perpendicular distance shrinks to nothing when the line passes through the bolt. Use the buttons to compare the two pushes.

lead.text: Sketch the line the force acts along, then find its perpendicular distance from the bolt.

Moments become useful when more than one force acts on a body. Take a see-saw with its pivot in the middle and a child at each end. One child turns it anticlockwise and the other clockwise. If the two moments are equal, they cancel and the see-saw stays level. Engineers call this equilibrium, as in the first lesson. The moments about the pivot add up to zero, with anticlockwise positive and clockwise negative.

The simplest balanced case has two children at equal distances from the pivot. The distances are equal, so the moments can only be equal if the forces are, which means the children weigh the same. A child's weight is a force, the pull of gravity, acting downwards at the seat.
Think about what must be equal for the two moments to cancel.

Now bring one child closer to the pivot. A heavy child sitting near the middle can balance a lighter child sitting far out, because the shorter distance makes up for the greater weight. Balance still means equal moments: the weight times the distance on one side equals the weight times the distance on the other.

A 200 N child 1.5 m from the pivot has a moment of 300 N·m. A 300 N child 1 m on the other side also has 300 N·m, so the see-saw balances. The picture shows that pair, and what happens when the heavier child moves out to the same distance as the lighter one.

afterFigure.text: This is the working rule for the rest of the course. Write down the moment of each force about the pivot, with its sign, add them up and set the total to zero. Whatever is unknown can then be found.

lead.text: The 300 N child stays where they are, and the heavier child can sit anywhere on the other side.

blocks.text: A wheel nut is stuck fast. You fit a short spanner and push with all your weight, and nothing moves. You swap it for a long wrench and the nut gives. You pushed no harder than before, yet the long handle did what the short one could not.

That everyday experience is the basis for much of engineering. It explains why a crane with a long arm needs a heavy block at the back and why a door handle sits as far from the hinges as it can. In every case a force acts at a distance from a point, and the distance matters as much as the force.
This lesson starts with the stuck nut and works out what decides how hard a push turns it. We then tilt the push, aim it at the nut itself, and finish by using the same idea to balance a see-saw.

diagram.alt: A spanner on a nut, seen from above, with a downward push at the end of the handle. A short handle is shown first and a long handle second. The push is the same size in both and only the distance from the nut changes.
diagram.caption: The same push on a short handle and on a long one. The longer the handle, the harder the nut is turned. Use the buttons to compare the two.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find how hard a force turns a body about a point, and use it to balance a beam.

recap.keyIdea: A moment is force times perpendicular distance from the pivot, and a body at rest has moments that cancel.

blocks.text: Back at the stuck bolt, you found that a 150 N push at right angles, 0.3 m from the bolt, gives 45 N·m. Tilting it to 30° cuts the moment to 22.5 N·m. You balanced a see-saw by matching a 300 N child's 600 N·m with a 400 N child at 1.5 m.

recap.nextHook: A beam resting on two supports is a see-saw whose pivot has been replaced by a pair of posts, and the next lesson works out how much each post carries.

questions.prompt: A see-saw balances with a 300 N child sitting 2 m from the pivot on one side. The other child also sits 2 m from the pivot, on the other side. How heavy is that child, in newtons?
hints: Each sits the same distance from the middle.
What would tip the see-saw if the weights differed?
Equal distances need equal weights.
questions.onCorrect: 300 N. At equal distances, equal moments need equal weights. Next: what if the distances differ?

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two weights. Balance needs the two sides to turn the see-saw equally.
Half the weight would only balance at twice the distance. Both children sit the same distance out.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Equal distances from the pivot balance only if the weights are equal, so the other child also weighs 300 N.

questions.prompt: Which change doubles the moment of a push on a spanner?
hints: M = F × d. Which letter does each option change?
questions.onCorrect: M = F × d, so doubling the perpendicular distance doubles the moment.

misconceptions.feedback: Half the force halves the moment. Moment is force times distance.
A push along the handle has no distance at right angles to it, so it does not turn the bolt.

choices.label: Push at twice the distance from the bolt
Push along the handle instead of across it

acceptedIdeas: Push at twice the distance from the bolt
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Push at twice the distance from the bolt. Doubling d doubles M = F × d.

questions.prompt: A 150 N force pushes at right angles to a spanner, 0.3 m from the bolt. Find the moment about the bolt in N·m.
hints: The push is already at right angles, so the full distance counts.
Multiply force by perpendicular distance.
Calculate 150 × 0.3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force alone. A moment multiplies it by the distance too.
That divides the force by the distance. A moment multiplies them.

questions.prompt: Why does only 90 sin 30° count towards the moment?
hints: Which part of the force could swing the handle round?
questions.onCorrect: The part along the handle has no turning effect. Only the part across it does.

misconceptions.feedback: A push at right angles needs no sine at all. Sine appears here because of the angle to the spanner.
Size is not the reason. The part along the handle is a real force but has no turning effect.

choices.label: Only the part of the force across the spanner turns it.
Sine is used for every moment, whatever the angle.
The bolt is only affected by the smaller part of any force.

acceptedIdeas: Only the part of the force across the spanner turns it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the part of the force across the spanner turns it.. The component along the spanner does not turn it; the component across it does.

hints: The turning part is 75 N. How far along the spanner does it act?
Multiply the turning part by the distance.
Calculate 75 × 0.3.
questions.onCorrect: 22.5 N·m: less than at right angles, because only part of the push turns the spanner.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the moment for a push at right angles. At 30° only part of it turns the spanner.
That uses cos 30°, the part along the handle, which does not turn it.

questions.prompt: A 200 N force pulls along a spanner's handle, directly away from the bolt, at a point 0.3 m from it. Find its moment about the bolt in N·m.
hints: Sketch the line of action of the force.
Measure the perpendicular distance from the bolt to that line.
Multiply the force by that distance.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The line of action passes through the bolt, so the perpendicular distance and the moment are both zero.

questions.onCorrect: A line of action through the pivot has no arm, so the moment vanishes whatever the force.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the force by the distance along the handle. A moment uses the distance at right angles to the line of action.

questions.prompt: A 300 N child sits 2 m left of a see-saw's pivot. How far right of the pivot, in metres, must a 400 N child sit for the see-saw to balance?
hints: The two moments about the pivot must be equal and opposite.
Find the left child's moment, then divide by the right child's weight.
Calculate 300 × 2 ÷ 400.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Balance needs 400 × d = 300 × 2 = 600 N·m, so d = 1.5 m.

questions.onCorrect: 1.5 m. The heavier child sits closer, so that both moments are equal.

misconceptions.feedback: Equal distances only balance equal weights. The heavier child needs a shorter arm.
That divides by the wrong weight. Divide the left moment by the right child's weight.

questions.prompt: A door handle is 0.8 m from the hinges. It is pulled with 40 N at right angles to the door. Find the moment about the hinges in N·m.
hints: The hinge line is the pivot.
The pull is perpendicular, so use the full 0.8 m.
Calculate 40 × 0.8.
questions.onCorrect: 32 N·m: force times its perpendicular distance from the hinges.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the force and the distance. A moment multiplies them.
That divides the force by the distance. A moment multiplies them.

questions.prompt: A 60 N force acts on a 0.5 m wrench at 30° to the wrench. Find the moment about the nut in N·m.
hints: Which part of the 60 N acts across the wrench?
That part is 60 × sin 30°.
Multiply it by 0.5 m.
questions.onCorrect: 15 N·m: only the part across the wrench, 60 sin 30°, multiplies the full distance.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the push as fully at right angles. Only the part across the wrench turns it.
That uses cos 30°, the part along the wrench, which does not turn it.

questions.prompt: To loosen a tight nut with the least effort, where and how should you push on the spanner?
hints: Moment is force times perpendicular distance. Make that distance as large as you can.

acceptedIdeas: At the end of the handle, at right angles to it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At the end of the handle, at right angles to it. The largest perpendicular distance gives the largest moment, and only a push at right angles uses all of it.

choices.label: At the end of the handle, at right angles to it
Near the nut, at right angles to the handle
